# ASCII Art

Adapted for Phantasy from the Hermes `creative/ascii-art` skill. Use it for title cards, terminal promos, social snippets, tool output flourishes, and quick art treatments that do not need motion. If the request is animated, switch to `ascii-video`.

## Tool Picker

- Text banner: use `pyfiglet` locally when available; otherwise use the Asciified API.
- Character with speech bubble: use `cowsay` or `cowthink`.
- Decorative border/frame: use `boxes`.
- ANSI-colored terminal treatment: use `toilet`.
- Raster image to ASCII: use `ascii-image-converter` first, `jp2a` for lightweight JPEG-only cases.
- Pre-made subject art: search `ascii.co.uk` and extract `<pre>` blocks.

## Text Banner Workflow

Local first:

```bash
python3 -m pyfiglet "PHANTASY" -f slant
python3 -m pyfiglet "PHANTASY" -f doom -w 100
python3 -m pyfiglet --list_fonts
```

Remote fallback:

```bash
curl -s "https://asciified.thelicato.io/api/v2/ascii?text=Phantasy&font=Slant"
curl -s "https://asciified.thelicato.io/api/v2/fonts"
```

Good font defaults:

- `slant`: clean, readable headers
- `doom`: heavy titles
- `small`: longer strings
- `cyberlarge`: overtly techy titles
- `3-d`: splash art

## Decorative Treatments

Speech bubble:

```bash
cowsay "Your companion is live"
cowsay -f tux "Deploy complete"
```

Border/frame:

```bash
echo "Launch sequence ready" | boxes -d stone
echo "Phantasy" | boxes -d diamonds
```

ANSI color:

```bash
toilet --gay "PHANTASY"
toilet -F border --metal "LIVE"
```

Combined treatment:

```bash
python3 -m pyfiglet "PHANTASY" -f slant | boxes -d stone
```

## Image to ASCII

Preferred tool:

```bash
ascii-image-converter image.png -C
ascii-image-converter image.png -d 80,40
ascii-image-converter image.png --save-txt output
```

Fallback:

```bash
jp2a --width=100 image.jpg
jp2a --colors image.jpg
```

## Search Existing Art

```bash
curl -s "https://ascii.co.uk/art/cat" -o /tmp/ascii_art.html
```

Then extract the `<pre>` blocks and keep only the strongest candidates. Clean HTML entities before returning the art.

## Style Rules

- Offer 2-3 variations when the user wants branding or taste input.
- Short text supports heavier fonts; long text needs tighter fonts.
- Prefer decorative framing only when it adds intent, not noise.
- If the output will be copied into plain text, avoid ANSI-only color effects.
- For video title cards or looping terminal visuals, escalate to `ascii-video`.

# ASCII Video

Adapted for Phantasy from the Hermes `creative/ascii-video` skill. Use it for stylized loops, music visualizers, teaser clips, terminal-native promos, lyric videos, and glitchy companion media where characters are the rendering medium.

## Preconditions

Run the setup check first through the Phantasy skill runtime:

```json
{ "name": "ascii-video", "mode": "setup_check" }
```

Required in practice:

- Python 3
- `numpy`
- `Pillow`
- `ffmpeg`

Common optional upgrades:

- `scipy` for richer FFT/audio analysis
- `opencv-python` for video frame sampling
- a TTS provider if the piece needs narration

## Creative Standard

- ASCII is the medium, not the gimmick.
- Build one coherent visual world across the whole video.
- Do not ship flat black frames with a single effect pasted on top.
- Every section should vary in palette, density, or motion vocabulary.
- Invent at least one project-specific treatment instead of reusing catalog defaults unchanged.

## Modes

- Video-to-ASCII: source footage becomes animated character output
- Audio-reactive: FFT-driven visualizer from music or narration
- Generative: pure procedural motion without source media
- Hybrid: source video with reactive overlays or shader passes
- Lyrics/text: timed captions, quotes, or typewriter overlays
- TTS narration: generated voice plus motion-driven text treatment

Open references only when that part of the build is active:

- Renderer architecture and palettes: `references/architecture.md`
- Layering, tonemap, masks, feedback: `references/composition.md`
- Effect vocabulary and particle systems: `references/effects.md`
- Audio, video, image, and text inputs: `references/inputs.md`
- Scene table and composition patterns: `references/scenes.md`
- Shaders, transitions, and output modes: `references/shaders.md`
- Performance tuning: `references/optimization.md`
- Failure modes: `references/troubleshooting.md`

## Core Pipeline

```text
INPUT -> ANALYZE -> SCENE_FN -> TONEMAP -> SHADE -> ENCODE
```

1. Load the source material or generate synthetic drivers.
2. Extract per-frame features such as bands, beats, luminance, motion, or timed text.
3. Render the ASCII scene into a pixel canvas.
4. Normalize brightness with adaptive tonemapping.
5. Apply feedback/shader passes.
6. Pipe frames to `ffmpeg` and mux audio if needed.

## Phantasy Workflow

1. Start with the concept: mood, palette family, text texture, and scene progression.
2. Choose resolution and aspect ratio for the destination surface.
3. Write one self-contained `renderer.py`.
4. Test a few timestamps or still frames before full export. Use `skill_run`, not generic shell, so Phantasy resolves the builtin skill directory and approval metadata correctly:

```json
{ "name": "ascii-video", "mode": "run" }
```

5. Render clips in segments if the video has distinct scenes.
6. Stitch, mux audio, and only then do final polish.

Recommended project layout:

```text
ascii-project/
  concept.md
  renderer.py
  clips/
  output/
  tmp/
```

## Implementation Rules

- Prefer multiple ASCII grids with different cell sizes for depth.
- Use adaptive tonemap instead of multiplying raw brightness.
- Build scenes as functions with explicit state, not random code in the main loop.
- Keep palette, feedback, and shader choices scene-aware.
- Validate Unicode palettes against the selected font before a full render.
- Prefer the repo-local wrapper when rendering so the shared video venv is on PATH.
- Redirect long-running `ffmpeg` stderr to a file to avoid pipe deadlocks.
- For a quick feelings clip, read `templates/feeling-renderer.py`, copy it to `renderer.py` in the command working directory, customize the palette/text, then call `skill_run`.

## Review Loop

- Render representative frames first.
- Check mean brightness before blaming the effect logic.
- If text overlays are unreadable, darken the backdrop region instead of cranking font size alone.
- If a scene feels generic, change the compositional idea, not just the colors.
- If the render is slow, simplify the character pass before trimming the artistic idea.

# FFmpeg

Use `ffmpeg` for practical media operations from the terminal: convert formats, trim clips, stitch assets, extract frames, and mux audio/video into release-ready outputs.

## Installation

```bash
# macOS
brew install ffmpeg

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y ffmpeg
```

## Common Tasks

```bash
# Convert video format
ffmpeg -i input.mov output.mp4

# Trim a clip
ffmpeg -ss 00:00:05 -to 00:00:20 -i input.mp4 -c copy trimmed.mp4

# Extract audio
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vn -acodec copy output.m4a

# Resize for web delivery
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf scale=1280:-2 -c:v libx264 -crf 23 -preset medium output.mp4

# Extract frames
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 frames/frame-%04d.png

# Combine video and audio
ffmpeg -i video.mp4 -i narration.wav -c:v copy -c:a aac -shortest final.mp4
```

## Guidance

- Prefer `-c copy` when you only need trimming or remuxing without re-encoding.
- Use `libx264` plus a reasonable `-crf` value for broadly compatible MP4 exports.
- Keep source files untouched and write outputs to new paths.
- For long-running jobs, capture stderr to a log file if you need progress diagnostics.

# Find My

Adapted for Phantasy from the Hermes Find My skill. Apple does not expose a general-purpose CLI for Find My, so this skill relies on macOS automation plus screenshots of the app.

## Preconditions

- macOS with Find My signed into the user’s iCloud account
- Screen Recording permission for the terminal
- `osascript` and `screencapture` available
- Optional: `peekaboo` installed for cleaner UI automation

Check availability first:

```bash
command -v osascript && command -v screencapture
```

## Core Workflow

```bash
# Open Find My
osascript -e 'tell application "FindMy" to activate'
sleep 3

# Capture the active window
screencapture -w -o /tmp/findmy.png
```

After capture, inspect the screenshot with a vision-capable model or another image-reading path instead of guessing locations from automation output alone.

## Optional Peekaboo Flow

```bash
peekaboo see --app "FindMy" --annotate --path /tmp/findmy-ui.png
peekaboo image --app "FindMy" --path /tmp/findmy-detail.png
```

## Rules

1. Use this only for devices or items the user owns or explicitly controls.
2. Keep Find My visible if tracking an AirTag over time; backgrounded views may stop refreshing.
3. Prefer screenshot analysis over pretending the app has a reliable structured API.

# GitHub CLI (gh)

Manage GitHub issues, pull requests, repositories, and more from the command line.

## Installation

```bash
# macOS
brew install gh

# Linux
curl -fsSL https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg | sudo dd of=/usr/share/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg] https://cli.github.com/packages stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list > /dev/null
sudo apt update
sudo apt install gh

# Windows
winget install GitHub.cli
```

## Authentication

```bash
gh auth login
```

## Issues

```bash
# List issues
gh issue list

# Create issue
gh issue create --title "Bug: Login fails" --body "Steps to reproduce..."

# View issue
gh issue view 123

# Close issue
gh issue close 123
```

## Pull Requests

```bash
# Create PR
gh pr create --title "Fix login bug" --body "This PR fixes..."

# List PRs
gh pr list
gh pr status

# View PR
gh pr view 45

# Checkout PR locally
gh pr checkout 45

# Merge PR
gh pr merge 45 --admin --squash
```

## Repositories

```bash
# Clone repo
gh repo clone owner/repo

# View repo info
gh repo view

# Create repo
gh repo create my-new-repo --public
```

## Gists

```bash
# Create gist
echo "hello world" | gh gist create

# List gists
gh gist list
```

## Tips

- Use `gh help` for full documentation
- Use `--jq` for JSON output parsing
- Use `--web` to open in browser

# iMessage

Adapted for Phantasy from the Hermes Apple iMessage skill. Use it when the user wants to read or send messages through macOS Messages.app from the terminal.

## Preconditions

- macOS with Messages.app signed in
- `imsg` installed
- Full Disk Access for the terminal if macOS requests it
- Automation permission for Messages.app when prompted

Check availability first:

```bash
command -v imsg
```

## When To Use

- Send a text or iMessage to a known recipient
- Review recent chats or message history
- Attach a local file to a message
- Watch a conversation for new incoming messages

## When Not To Use

- Non-Apple messaging services such as Telegram, Discord, Slack, or WhatsApp
- Bulk messaging or anything that looks like spam
- Unknown recipients without explicit user confirmation

## Quick Reference

```bash
# List recent chats
imsg chats --limit 10 --json

# Read recent history
imsg history --chat-id 1 --limit 20 --json

# Send a text
imsg send --to "+14155551212" --text "Hello!"

# Send with an attachment
imsg send --to "+14155551212" --text "See attached" --file /path/to/file.jpg

# Watch a chat for new messages
imsg watch --chat-id 1 --attachments
```

## Rules

1. Confirm the recipient and message body before sending.
2. Verify attachment paths before trying to send them.
3. Prefer `--json` output when inspecting chats programmatically.
4. Treat mass or repeated outbound messaging as approval-sensitive.

# Manim Video

Adapted for Phantasy from the Hermes `creative/manim-video` skill. Use it for companion explainers, lore/education shorts, algorithm walkthroughs, architecture diagrams, and data-story videos where programmatic animation is a better fit than screen recording.

## Preconditions

Run the setup check before promising a final render:

```bash
bash skills/manim-video/scripts/setup.sh
```

For real rendering you typically need:

- Python 3
- `manim` installed in the Python environment
- LaTeX (`pdflatex`) for `MathTex`
- `ffmpeg` for scene stitching and audio muxing

If prerequisites are missing, you can still:

- write the plan
- scaffold `script.py`
- draft subtitles and narration
- prepare the concat/audio pipeline

## Creative Standard

- Treat the piece as educational cinema, not slideware.
- Start from the misconception, tension, or question the viewer has.
- Show geometry or motion before burying the viewer in symbols.
- Leave breathing room after reveals with `self.wait()`.
- Keep one visual language across scenes: palette, type scale, timing.
- Use contrast intentionally: primary elements bright, context dim, scaffolding faint.

## Output Modes

- Concept explainer: animated intuition for a topic or mechanism
- Equation derivation: stepwise proof or symbolic transformation
- Algorithm visualization: state changes, swaps, traversals, counters
- Data story: animated charts, comparisons, deltas, milestones
- Architecture diagram: systems building up with labels and flows
- 3D visualization: camera motion around surfaces, fields, or structures

Open references only as needed:

- Scene planning: `references/scene-planning.md`
- Motion and timing: `references/animations.md`
- Layout and visual language: `references/visual-design.md`
- Math-heavy scenes: `references/equations.md`
- Graphs, plots, algorithms: `references/graphs-and-data.md`
- Camera, zoom, or 3D: `references/camera-and-3d.md`
- Render and stitch workflow: `references/rendering.md`
- Common failures: `references/troubleshooting.md`

## Phantasy Workflow

1. Write `plan.md` first with the narrative arc, scene order, palette, subtitle copy, and rough durations.
2. Build one `script.py` with one Manim class per scene.
3. Iterate in low quality first:

```bash
bash skills/manim-video/scripts/with-env.sh manim -ql script.py SceneName
```

4. Render the full set only after stills and timings are clean.
5. Stitch scene clips with `ffmpeg`.
6. Add narration or music only after the visual pacing is stable.

Suggested project layout:

```text
video-project/
  plan.md
  script.py
  concat.txt
  final.mp4
  media/
```

## Implementation Rules

- Define shared colors, fonts, and background constants at file top.
- Set `self.camera.background_color` in every scene.
- Use raw strings for LaTeX: `MathTex(r"\frac{1}{2}")`.
- Prefer clean scene exits with `FadeOut(Group(*self.mobjects))`.
- Use subtitles or subcaptions for every major beat.
- Iterate at `-ql`; reserve `-qh` for final output.
- Prefer the repo-local wrapper when rendering so the local venv and TeX install are on PATH:

```bash
bash skills/manim-video/scripts/with-env.sh manim -qh script.py SceneName
```

- If proportional fonts look broken, switch to a monospace family.

## Minimal Scene Skeleton

```python
from manim import *

BG = "#151515"
PRIMARY = "#58C4DD"
SECONDARY = "#83C167"
ACCENT = "#F6D860"
MONO = "Menlo"

class Intro(Scene):
    def construct(self):
        self.camera.background_color = BG
        title = Text(
            "Why This Works",
            font=MONO,
            font_size=48,
            color=PRIMARY,
            weight=BOLD,
        )
        self.add_subcaption("Why this works", duration=2)
        self.play(Write(title), run_time=1.5)
        self.wait(1.0)
        self.play(FadeOut(title), run_time=0.5)
```

## Review Loop

- Render a still or draft clip for each scene before full production.
- Check legibility at the actual export size.
- Confirm the pacing matches the plan, not just the code.
- If a scene feels cluttered, remove objects before adding more motion.
- If the render fails, use `references/troubleshooting.md` before rewriting the scene from scratch.

# Phantasy Extension Authoring

Use this skill when the task is to create or update a Phantasy extension surface.

## Choose The Right Surface

- Build a `plugin` when you need runtime hooks, tools, integrations, or executable capability boundaries.
- Build a `skill` when you need reusable instructions or workflow guidance for the agent without new runtime code.
- Build a `workflow` when the output is a reusable automation graph in `.workflow.json`.

## Preferred Commands

```bash
phantasy create plugin my-plugin --workspace operations --kind capability
phantasy create skill my-skill --workspace character --kind behavior
phantasy create workflow review-loop --template approval-loop
```

## Taxonomy Rules

- Every first-party extension must declare an owning workspace: `character`, `site`, `business`, `operations`, or the Workflows workspace (internal id `automations`).
- Use `capability` or `integration` for plugins, `behavior` for skills, and `automation` for workflows unless there is a strong reason otherwise.
- Prefer workspace-owned directories over transport-specific dumping grounds.

## Editing Guidance

1. Start from the scaffold instead of copying ad hoc files.
2. Keep the initial template lean; add scripts, references, or assets only when the extension genuinely needs them.
3. Preserve explicit local developer power in dedicated developer paths instead of silently enabling privileged tools for beginner product shapes.

# Phantasy Product Architecture

Use this skill when the task is to place, refactor, or name first-party Phantasy features.

## Core Model

- The repo is one flagship product: `WordPress for AI companions`.
- The five primary workspaces are:
  - `character`
  - `site`
  - `business`
  - `workflows` (internal id `automations`)
  - `operations`
- `Notifications` is a launcher and inbox surface, not a sixth architecture domain.

## Placement Rules

1. Decide the owning workspace first.
2. Decide whether the logic is:
   - trusted kernel
   - product surface
   - extension surface
3. Put domain logic before transport-specific wrappers.

Prefer:

- `workspaces/domain -> adapter surface`

Avoid:

- `admin-ui first -> domain later`
- registry-only indirection when shared metadata would solve the problem

## Kernel Versus Product

- Kernel: provider contracts, config, memory/storage interfaces, workflow execution, plugin contracts, orchestration primitives.
- Product: Character, Site, Business, Workflows, Operations features in admin UI, admin API, CLI, and public APIs.
- Extensions: plugins, skills, workflows, packages.

## Site-Specific Bias

For CMS and Site work:

- Skills are `behavior`
- Plugins are usually `capability` or `integration`
- Workflows are `automation`

Keep website/front-end rendering outside the first-party release surface; shared CMS features need a Site-domain model and public API contract.

## Taxonomy References

- `src/product/taxonomy.ts`
- `src/product/taxonomy-validation.ts`
- `src/plugins/content/plugin-metadata.ts`
- `src/site/public-content-service.ts`

## Naming Guidance

- Use plain product language in user-facing surfaces.
- Prefer `Content` over internal or poetic terms when the feature is really posts, pages, publishing, or CMS operations.
- Remove release-surface aliases for retired first-party features, and keep labels, tabs, and docs on current product language.

## Validation

When moving or introducing product surfaces, verify:

```bash
bun run typecheck
bun run validate:standards
```

# Phantasy Site Building

Use this skill when the task is to build or refactor the Phantasy Site workspace, headless CMS editor, pages, posts, public content APIs, media attachments, or block-based publishing flows.

## Product Framing

- Treat this as the `Site` workspace for the flagship product, not a detached blog tool.
- The companion is the protagonist; publishing and the CMS shell are supporting product surfaces around her.
- Prefer domain-first CMS primitives over transport-first hacks.

## Current Repo Shape

- The current Site system is the source of truth for document editing, publishing, and public content APIs.
- `Pages` and `Posts` live under the Site content model, not config-backed page blobs.
- Draft sessions, checkpoints, revisions, activity, media attachments, and blocks remain first-class CMS infrastructure.
- Bundled frontend delivery is out of scope for this repo; keep external frontends user-owned.

## Key Files

- Draft/worktree + git-backed editing: `src/site/workspace-service.ts`
- Site settings/types/schema: `src/site/types.ts`, `src/site/schemas.ts`
- Site admin API: `src/admin-api/routes/site/site-routes.ts`
- Public content APIs: `src/site/public-content-service.ts`, `src/server/routes/public-api-routes.ts`
- Block registry and HTML rendering: `src/site/block-registry.ts`
- Site admin UI: `src/admin-ui/components/tabs/SiteTab.tsx`

## Working Rules

1. Keep the Site workspace focused on CMS metadata, documents, media, checkpoints, revisions, drafts, publishing, and public read APIs.
2. Keep pages/posts as first-class site documents and avoid reintroducing config-backed page storage.
3. If adding a new first-party CMS feature, assign explicit Site workspace ownership and keep taxonomy metadata consistent.
4. Keep the public API stable for both structured `blocks` and rendered HTML `content`.
5. Treat frontend stacks as user-owned consumers of the headless APIs.

## Current Constraints To Remember

- Site drafts are git-backed; autosave is file persistence, while checkpoints are explicit draft-branch commits.
- `SiteSettings` should stay CMS metadata only: title, description, and language.
- Removed presentation config fields should not be generated, accepted in new schemas, or documented.
- Import and migration work should land on the current Site document/API path only.

## Preferred Direction

When improving the CMS, bias toward this architecture:

- Unify posts and pages into one Site-owned content model.
- Introduce explicit body formats or a canonical `body` object instead of ambiguous raw strings.
- Move toward block-capable content documents.
- Render document bodies through shared block helpers for the `content` HTML response.
- Preserve structured `blocks` in public responses so external frontends can render with their own components.

## Blocks Guidance

If the task mentions blocks, Gutenberg-like editing, or custom page building:

1. Start with a block registry and a renderer contract before building lots of block types.
2. Keep block definitions explicit: `type`, attributes, allowed children, and render behavior.
3. Support a migration path from current HTML and Markdown content.
4. Add a small core block set first:
   - paragraph
   - heading
   - image
   - quote
   - list
   - code
   - divider
   - button
   - group
   - columns
   - embed
   - custom-html
5. Make advanced blocks such as `custom-html` or script/embed surfaces privileged and explicit.
6. Prefer plugin-extensible blocks over hardcoding every block in the core editor.

## Editing Workflow

1. Identify whether the task belongs in Site settings, document editing, publishing, media, public API, or block infrastructure.
2. Inspect the existing CMS and content path before patching:
   - storage model
   - admin edit surface
   - public API shape
   - publish/visibility rules
3. If changing CMS data shape, update:
   - TypeScript types
   - admin API routes
   - UI editor/controller
   - public content API
   - relevant tests and generated docs
4. Do not preserve retired frontend delivery or presentation config paths.

## Avoid

- Treating config-backed pages as the final CMS architecture.
- Adding page-specific inline logic that should live in a renderer or block registry.
- Mixing frontend presentation concerns with storage or content-type policy.
- Giving unrestricted script execution to regular content authors by default.
- Reintroducing bundled frontend delivery or visual editing shells.

## Validation

Prefer targeted validation after CMS/site changes:

```bash
bun run test:core -- src/site
bun run test:core -- src/admin-api/routes/site
bun run test:ui:components -- src/admin-ui/components/tabs/site
bun run validate:standards
bun run typecheck
```

If the change touches broad CMS flows, also verify:

```bash
bun run test
```

# Research Paper Writing

Adapted for Phantasy from the Hermes `research/research-paper-writing` skill. Use it when a repo, experiment set, note pile, or half-written manuscript needs to become a coherent research paper rather than a generic blog post or README.

## Default Posture

- Draft first. Ask questions only when blocked by venue choice, missing evidence, or a genuinely ambiguous contribution.
- Never invent citations, metrics, reviewer comments, or author-guide rules. Use `[CITATION NEEDED]`, `[RESULT NEEDED]`, or `[CHECK AUTHOR GUIDE]` when verification is incomplete.
- Every section should support a paper claim, and every claim should point to evidence.
- Verify the live official author guide before locking page limits, anonymity rules, required sections, or camera-ready policy.

## Pick The Paper Type

- Empirical paper: claims map to experiments, ablations, and analysis.
- Theory paper: claims map to theorems, assumptions, and proofs, with optional empirical validation.
- Survey or position paper: claims map to taxonomy, synthesis, and argument structure.
- Benchmark or resource paper: claims map to task design, documentation, baselines, and intended use.

If the project mixes modes, choose one primary evidence style and let the rest support it.

## Phantasy Workflow

1. Audit the repo and manuscript surface.
   - Prefer `papers/<slug>/` for working files when you control the repo layout.
   - Inspect existing drafts, `references.bib`, figures, claim audits, experiment logs, and results directories before writing prose.
2. Create four anchor artifacts before a full draft.
   - One-sentence contribution.
   - Evidence map: `claim -> evidence -> remaining gap -> section`.
   - Venue note: target venue, current template or policy source, and submission constraints.
   - Outline with planned tables, figures, and appendix items.
3. Draft from the evidence inward.
   - Methods, setup, experiments, and figure captions first.
   - Results discussion next.
   - Introduction and abstract after the story is stable.
4. Run a reviewer pass.
   - Soundness, baseline fairness, theorem assumptions, missing related work, limitations, ethics, and reproducibility.
5. Package the submission.
   - Verified bibliography, readable figures, appendix or supplement, anonymization or camera-ready cleanup, and reproducibility details.

## Working Rules

- Group related work by idea, assumption, or evaluation regime, not paper-by-paper chronology.
- Put a claim sentence at the start of each experiment subsection: `This experiment tests whether ...`.
- Track provenance for every number so tables can be regenerated from source artifacts.
- If the evidence is weak, narrow the claim instead of inflating the prose.
- Prefer concrete output files such as `outline.md`, `evidence-map.md`, `paper.md`, or `paper.tex` over vague planning notes.

## Open References Only When Needed

- Project setup, contribution framing, and outline design: `references/project-setup-and-story.md`
- Citation workflow and related-work synthesis: `references/literature-and-citations.md`
- Claim-to-experiment design, analysis, and figure discipline: `references/experiments-analysis-and-figures.md`
- Self-review, rebuttal, and submission packaging: `references/review-and-submission.md`

## Venue Scope

Common targets include NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, AAAI, COLM, workshops, and journal resubmissions. Treat venue rules as live inputs, not static knowledge baked into the skill.

# xAI Grok

Use this skill when the user wants to configure, troubleshoot, or operate xAI
Grok models, Grok-backed web search, X search, Grok TTS, Grok Imagine, or
Hermes/OpenClaw-style xAI integration from Phantasy.

## Boundary

- This skill teaches the workflow. It does not itself add runtime tool access.
- If Phantasy has a first-party xAI provider/plugin available, use that as the
  executable surface and use this skill for setup, tool choice, and prompting.
- If the user asks for a new runtime integration, keep the split clear:
  provider/plugin code owns auth, API calls, tools, and UI; this skill owns
  guidance for agents and operators.
- Do not claim Phantasy supports xAI OAuth unless a Phantasy provider/plugin
  actually exposes that flow.

## Auth Choice

Prefer the path that matches the available runtime surface:

1. `XAI_API_KEY`: normal API-key path for OpenAI-compatible or xAI Responses
   transport. Use this when Phantasy is calling xAI directly today.
2. SuperGrok OAuth: browser OAuth 2.0 PKCE against `accounts.x.ai`, with a
   loopback callback and token refresh. Use this only when a runtime provider
   explicitly implements it.
3. Existing upstream runtime: for Hermes/OpenClaw migration or interop work,
   preserve that runtime's native config instead of flattening it into a
   Phantasy-only shape.

Credential rules:

- Put API keys in environment variables, secret stores, or encrypted runtime
  config; never write them to tracked files.
- Treat OAuth bearer and refresh tokens as secrets equal to API keys.
- In remote SSH/container sessions, a loopback OAuth callback must be reachable
  from the browser. If the callback binds on the remote host, forward the
  callback port before opening the auth URL locally.

## Surface Selection

Use the narrowest xAI surface that matches the task:

- General chat or reasoning: Grok chat model through the configured provider.
- Current web facts with citations: Grok web-grounded search.
- X/Twitter posts, threads, handles, or post metrics: X search. For metrics or
  a specific post, pass the exact post URL or status ID instead of a broad
  query.
- Speech output: Grok TTS if the runtime exposes a TTS tool/provider.
- Images or videos: Grok Imagine only when the runtime exposes image/video
  tools and the user requested generated media.
- Remote code execution: use xAI code execution only when the runtime exposes
  it clearly as remote sandbox execution. Do not describe it as local shell
  access.

For search tasks, ask the model for cited synthesis, not a raw search-result
dump. Grok search providers commonly return one synthesized answer with
citations rather than an N-result SERP.

## Model Policy

- Prefer the runtime's live model catalog over hardcoded names.
- If a default is needed and the catalog includes it, use `grok-4.3` for chat.
- For lower-latency search/tool loops, choose a fast Grok model from the
  runtime catalog rather than inventing a model id.
- Do not send OpenAI-only reasoning-effort or strict tool-schema options to a
  native xAI transport unless the provider adapter says they are supported.

## Phantasy Operating Loop

1. Check whether the active Phantasy runtime already has an xAI provider,
   plugin, MCP server, or tool registered.
2. If no executable xAI surface exists, tell the user what is missing and
   propose the smallest next integration: provider for chat, plugin for
   Phantasy-owned tools/auth/UI, or MCP only for external callable tools.
3. If an API-key path exists, confirm `XAI_API_KEY` or equivalent secret config
   is present before making live calls.
4. If an OAuth path exists, confirm the browser/loopback setup before starting
   the flow, especially on remote hosts.
5. Pick the surface from "Surface Selection".
6. Return cited results for search, generated media links for media tasks, and
   explicit caveats when xAI quota, subscription, or unsupported model/tool
   behavior blocks the request.

## Migration Notes

Hermes-style xAI OAuth:

- Provider identity is commonly named around `xai-oauth`.
- The flow is SuperGrok subscription based and does not use `XAI_API_KEY`.
- A single OAuth login can cover chat plus direct xAI media/search tools when
  the runtime wires those surfaces to the same token.

OpenClaw-style xAI:

- The common path is API-key first via `XAI_API_KEY`.
- xAI search usually splits into Grok-backed `web_search` for web-grounded
  answers and `x_search` for X/Twitter content.
- Treat OpenClaw `code_execution` as a remote xAI sandbox, not host execution.

When importing or documenting either runtime, keep auth semantics intact:
OAuth subscription quota and paid API-key quota are different operator choices.

## Avoid

- Do not store `XAI_API_KEY`, OAuth access tokens, or refresh tokens in
  `SKILL.md`, docs examples with real values, git-tracked config, or logs.
- Do not enable broad X monitoring or posting workflows just because search is
  configured. Reading/searching X and posting to X are different Business
  permissions.
- Do not pretend an xAI search skill is a provider plugin. If the model needs
  executable search, the runtime still needs a registered tool.
- Do not route companion private memories, transcripts, or customer data into
  live web/X searches unless the user explicitly asks and the runtime policy
  allows it.
